_readme: Scout notes for the twelfth photo batch (Oct 23, 2026): photos for the 20 volume-20 pages (data/god-build/research/volume-20-2026-10-23.md), chosen to show each subject where people find it: bites on skin, bugs at windows, doors, walls and floors, nests on houses, pests in food, shrews in yards and basements. Same format as batches 7 to 11: for each photo, what its source says it shows and who identified it (sourceDescription), the pages it serves (forPages; slugs as in plan.src.json, learn/<slug> for the Learning Centre, tools/<slug> for a reader tool; 'wheel-bugs' is the planned slug the selector re-aims at 'assassin bug'), confidence in the identification, whether it can be a page's lead/share image (leadEligible: true only for public domain or CC0 AND a confident identification of what the page is about), and caveats. The licence, credit and size of record are in photos.json. 58 photos were added, with no script change beyond the 58 PHOTOS rows: 7 public domain (6 CDC PHIL, 1 USGS via Commons), 15 CC0, 33 CC BY 4.0, 1 CC BY-SA 4.0 and 2 CC BY-SA 3.0. Identifications: every iNaturalist photo is research grade with at least one identifier besides the observer; the rest are CDC PHIL records (CDC's own description and attribution), a USGS lab photo and two Commons bite photos (see their confidence fields). Bite photos are clinical or credited: CDC PHIL (cat flea bites attributed by CDC, fire ant stings), a photo credited 'James Heilman, MD', and one photographer's own bites that he attributes to bed bugs (marked as such). All 58 images were looked at large before choosing and again after conversion, and show what their subject lines say. A read-only replica of the lib/photos.ts and lib/guides.ts rules was run against the 58 new records: every licence is in LICENSE_LABEL, every file is on disk at its recorded size, the 22 public domain and CC0 photos pass shareImage(), the 36 CC BY and CC BY-SA photos need their visible credit, and photoCreator() types the USGS credit as an Organization and gives no creator for the six PHIL records (they name a content provider, not a photographer). The ledger change is additive: 421 records before, 479 after, none changed. Sizes: two files stay over the script's 260 KB target at its lowest quality (termite-swarmers-ceiling-light 322 KB, giant-water-bug-brick-pavement 292 KB; textured surfaces compress poorly) and two are small (booklouse-cereal-package 676 x 689, wheel-bug-nymphs-hatching-wall 1004 x 713). Several observers' place names carry a street address or a school's name: the caveats say what may be printed. Photos now on file per page (new in brackets): jumping spiders 5 (+3), orb weavers 7 (+2), camel spiders 4 (+3), joro spiders 4 (+3), flea bites 3 bite photos (+2) plus a flea on a fingertip (+1) and the flea-on-pet photos from batch 10, bed bug bites 5 (+3), ant bites and fire ant stings 5 (+4), paper wasps 5 (+2), mud daubers 5 (+2), wheel and other assassin bugs 8 (+3), giant water bugs 4 (+4), weevils 6 (+4), booklice 4 (+3), carpet beetle larvae 6 (+3), pill bugs 4 (+3), Jerusalem crickets 3 (+3), fruit flies 4 (+1), drain flies 5 (+2), termites 11 (+3), shrews 4 (+4). Every topic now has at least 3 photos, at least 2 of them where people find it. Leads (public domain or CC0 and confidently identified): what-do-bed-bug-bites-look-like: bed-bug-on-skin-cdc (the bites themselves are CC BY-SA, or bed-bug-bites-back from batch 7, CC0, self-reported); flea-bites: flea-bites-ankles-cdc; fire-ant-stings: fire-ant-stings-pustules-closeup; do-carpenter-ants-bite: carpenter-ant-on-fingers; jumping-spiders: zebra-jumping-spider-house-wall or bold-jumping-spider (batch 3); camel-spiders: camel-spider-apartment-floor; joro-spiders: joro-spider-front-door; wheel-bugs/assassin-bugs: wheel-bug-on-fingers; water-bugs-vs-cockroaches: giant-water-bug-brick-pavement; weevils: maize-weevil-fingertip; carpet-beetle-larvae: carpet-beetle-larva-hallway-wall; pill-bugs: pill-bugs-in-palm; jerusalem-crickets: jerusalem-cricket-wood-floor; how-to-get-rid-of-drain-flies: drain-fly-bathroom-wall; shrews: short-tailed-shrew-snout-usgs (a dead specimen: a live CC BY photo reads better in the page, but cannot be the share image). Paper wasps, mud daubers, booklice and fruit flies keep their earlier CC0 or public domain leads (dark-paper-wasp, paper-wasp-nest, black-and-yellow-mud-dauber, blue-mud-dauber-on-nest, booklouse, fruit-fly). Searches, refused candidates, alternatives and what is still missing are in 'gaps'. Write captions from these notes and the record together, in US spelling and US units. No page or lib file was edited in this batch.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 164065154, Glendale, Salt Lake City, Utah, 2023-05-27, by Rebecca Ray (tigerbb; about 137,000 identifications). Observer's note: the spider 'has been living in our house for months now. He likes it in the kitchen window but also spends a lot of time around our plants.' Eleven current identifications, all Phidippus audax, including jumping_arachnids (about 167,000 identifications), calebcam (about 237,000) and Sam Kieschnick (about 863,000). Photo 1 of 1.
candidates.caveats: A black bold jumping spider with white spots and blue-green iridescent mouthparts (chelicerae), legs spread on window glass, a white window frame at the right and garden greenery blurred outside. That this is the kitchen window of the house it lived in is the observer's account: say 'on a kitchen window'. The observer calls it 'he'; nobody annotated the sex: don't state it. A strand of silk crosses the top. No scale object. CC BY: credit Rebecca Ray.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Rebecca Ray, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x1331.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 206175475, Buckingham Springs, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, 2024-04-08, by Bill Keim (keimwj; about 21,000 observations). Observer's note: 'Found on siding.' Identified to the genus Phidippus by the observer and spiderladylyle (Breanna Lyle, about 382,000 identifications), and to Phidippus audax by jumping_arachnids (about 167,000) and huttonia (Matthew Lindsey, about 140,000). Photo 1 of 2.
candidates.caveats: An orange-brown, hairy bold jumping spider with green iridescent chelicerae on white grooved vinyl siding in sunlight; sharp. Its color differs from the black adult in bold-jumping-spider-kitchen-window: bold jumping spiders vary with age and sex, but cite a source before saying which this is (no life stage or sex is recorded). No scale object. CC BY: credit Bill Keim.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Bill Keim, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x800.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 76237466, Logy Bay-Middle Cove-Outer Cove, Newfoundland and Labrador, 2021-05-01, by Mardon Erbland (logybayer). Observer's note: '5.5 mm nose to body rear. Found sitting on the side of our house.' Identified as Salticus scenicus by the observer, arthropop and calebcam (about 237,000 identifications). Photo 1 of 2; CC0.
candidates.caveats: A black-and-white striped zebra jumping spider on a white, slightly speckled painted surface (the house wall, by the observer's note); sharp dorsal view. The 5.5 mm length is the observer's measurement: attribute it, or use a published size range. A Canadian location is fine for a US page (the species is common on house walls in the northern US too: cite a source for the range). CC0 and confidently identified: a lead option for jumping-spiders.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1160.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 19186831, Lake Forest Park, Washington (a street address), 2018-12-23, by John Brew (brewbooks; about 24,000 observations). Identified as Araneus diadematus by the observer and Stewart Wechsler (about 142,000 identifications). Photo 1 of 3.
candidates.caveats: A cross orbweaver hanging in its web, seen from below (the white cross on the back does not show), with gray house siding and a window frame blurred behind. Whether the web is outside the glass is not stated: say 'at the corner of a kitchen window'. A December record. Do not print the street address. 1070 x 805. CC BY: credit John Brew.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) John Brew, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1070x805.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 243698225, Hamilton, Ohio (a street name), 2024-09-23, by Mary Spilman (maryspilman). Observer's note: 'Has reconstructed a web across my back door every night for two months, just to be torn down again in the morning.' Identified as Larinioides cornutus by the observer, huttonia (Matthew Lindsey, about 140,000 identifications) and spiderladylyle (Breanna Lyle, about 382,000). Photo 1 of 2.

The spider is small in the frame: the picture's value is the setting, a web rebuilt across a door every night (the observer's account). Do not print the street name. CC BY: credit Mary Spilman.

candidates.confidence: high for a solifuge (order Solifugae); species Eremocosta striata by two identifiers, genus confirmed by a third
candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 6763128, Sierra Vista, Arizona (a street address), 2017-06-22, by CK2AZ (about 338,000 observations). No description. Identified as Eremocosta striata by the observer and Kari McWest (kjmcwest); to the genus Eremocosta by solifugaeworldwide01 (Sebastian Garza Maya, about 15,000 identifications); to the family Eremobatidae and the order Solifugae by two more. Photo 2 of 5.
candidates.caveats: A pale tan solifuge with a dark-banded abdomen on a heavily textured white wall (stucco or textured drywall), a fingertip pointing at it from the lower left for scale. Whether this is inside or outside is not recorded: say 'on a house wall' (the place is a house address, not to be printed). 2017 photo, 1762 x 1321 original. CC BY: credit CK2AZ.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) CK2AZ, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x900.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 67964825, Key West, Florida, 2021-01-11, by Marissa Balfour (marissa3). Observer's note: 'These guys like living in my apartment apparently. Third one we've found here. Missing a leg.' Six identifications, all Ammotrechella stimpsoni, including myriada (David Hernandez, about 128,000 identifications), mecopteron_bouillon (Ahn Feldman, about 44,000), dum1 (about 69,000) and waye2go. Photo 2 of 2; CC0.
candidates.caveats: A dark-bodied solifuge on a speckled tan floor (tile or terrazzo by our reading) in the observer's apartment. It is missing a leg (the observer's note): don't use it to count legs. The Florida camel spider belongs to a different family (Ammotrechidae) from the western Eremobatidae in camel-spider-house-wall and camel-spider-in-hand. An identifier wrote on the observer's sister record (47551139) that it is the only solifuge recorded in Florida according to Muma (1967): cite a published source, not the comment. CC0: a lead option for a 'camel spider in the house' slot.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1200.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 174063588, Pima County, Arizona, 2023-07-20, by Wendy McCrady (wendybirds; about 34,000 observations). Identified as Eremocosta striata by solifugaeworldwide01 (Sebastian Garza Maya, about 15,000 identifications) and the observer. Photo 1 of 3.
candidates.caveats: A large tan solifuge with big jaws (chelicerae) on an open palm at an insect event (the observer writes 'IECC' without expanding it: don't expand). Whose hand it is is not stated. Useful for 'how big is a camel spider'. Don't let the photo suggest handling them: solifuges can bite (cite a source). CC BY: credit Wendy McCrady.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Wendy McCrady, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x1115.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 97032719, Georgia (location shown to state level), 2021-10-02, by janeyair (about 113,000 identifications). Observer's note: 'Side of house'. Identified as Trichonephila clavata by the observer, pucak (Joan Knapp, about 410,000 identifications), presto84 and wthompson23 (W. Thompson, about 129,000). Photo 3 of 4; CC0.
candidates.caveats: A large golden web hanging from a roof gutter down the outside corner of a house, shingles above; the spider is small, up by the gutter. The setting is the point (how big and how close to the house joro webs get); not a lead (the spider barely shows: use joro-spider or joro-spider-front-door). Same observer and house as joro-spider-front-door, a day apart: don't present them as two places.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1316.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 97032775, Georgia (state level), 2021-10-03, by janeyair. Observer's note: 'Front door'. Five identifications, all Trichonephila clavata (the observer, pucak, presto84, wthompson23 and dreakicks). Observation field 'Joro Leg Color Morph - Solid Black': 'Solid Black'. Photo 1 of 2; CC0.
candidates.caveats: A female joro (by size and the yellow-banded abdomen; cite a source for the sexes) in her golden web against beige house siding, reddish trim at the lower left; phone photo, slightly soft. Same observer and house as joro-spider-web-gutter. CC0 and confidently identified: a lead option for joro-spiders beside the batch-3 joro-spider.
candidates.note: Credit: no rights reserved, via iNaturalist. Licence: CC0-1.0. Size: 1200x1378.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 131123271, Clarkston, Georgia, 2022-08-16, by Laura Martin (sugarbuns). Observer's note: 'Saw this pair outside the house'. Identified as Trichonephila clavata by the observer, greatpurpleheron and pucak (Joan Knapp, about 410,000 identifications), who adds 'Female (large) and male (small)'. Photo 1 of 1.
candidates.caveats: A large female (yellow-banded abdomen, long banded legs) and a much smaller brown male above her, in a web against white painted trim or a soffit, a few dark spots on the paint. The female/male labels come from pucak's identification comment: attribute them, or cite a source that males are much smaller. 1103 x 939. CC BY: credit Laura Martin.

candidates.confidence: clinical record: CDC describes the lesions as attributed to cat flea bites
candidates.sourceDescription: CDC PHIL 25258, content provider CDC/Dr. H.G. Scott; PHIL's rights field says public domain. PHIL's description: an anterosuperior view of a female patient's lower legs and feet 'highlighting the presence of numerous erythematous macular lesions, which had been attributed to flea bites, inflicted by the cat flea, Ctenocephalides felis', captured in Decatur, Georgia, in 1963; PHIL 25257 to 25260 are four views of this patient.
candidates.caveats: Black and white (sepia-toned): the redness does not show, the bites read as dark dots. Both lower legs from the front, the woman seated in 1960s pointed shoes on a tiled floor; the bites cluster around the ankles and lower legs (cite CDC or a dermatology source for where flea bites cluster). Keep CDC's wording ('bites attributed to cat fleas') and say it is a 1963 photo. Public domain and a clinical attribution: lead-eligible for flea-bites, though a color photo may read better in the page.
candidates.note: Credit: CDC/ Dr. H.G. Scott (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov). Licence: public-domain. Size: 1200x1763.

candidates.confidence: clinical record: same CDC patient and attribution
candidates.sourceDescription: CDC PHIL 25257, same patient and content provider (CDC/Dr. H.G. Scott; Decatur, Georgia, 1963); public domain per PHIL. A left superolateral view of the patient's left lower leg and foot, 'highlighting the presence of numerous erythematous macular lesions, which had been attributed to flea bites, inflicted by the cat flea, Ctenocephalides felis'.
candidates.caveats: The closer view: clusters of dark spots on the ankle and the top of the foot above the shoe; sepia-toned. Use with flea-bites-ankles-cdc or instead of it, not as a separate case. The other views in the series were looked at and not taken (see gaps).
candidates.note: Credit: CDC/ Dr. H.G. Scott (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov). Licence: public-domain. Size: 1200x1196.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 371364750, Fort Worth, Texas, 2026-06-13, by Sam Kieschnick (sambiology; about 189,000 observations, 863,000 identifications). Observer's note: 'Shoot! Fleas on the cats. Will have to do some treatment.' Four identifications, all Ctenocephalides felis (jrpletch, the observer, castlegrande, texas_nature_family). Photo 1 of 4.
candidates.caveats: A cat flea in side view on finely ridged skin (a fingertip by our reading): the flattened body, combs and long hind legs show. It shows a flea on a person, not a bite. That the fleas came off his cats is the observer's note. Small file (1024 x 768). CC BY: credit Sam Kieschnick.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) Sam Kieschnick, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1024x768.

candidates.confidence: high (CDC: common bed bug, Cimex lectularius)
candidates.sourceDescription: CDC PHIL 6283, content provider 'CDC/ Donated by the World Health Organization, Geneva, Switzerland'; PHIL's rights field says public domain. Description: 'a left lateral view of a common bed bug, Cimex lectularius, which was photographed as it was perched atop the skin of its human host'.
candidates.caveats: A reddish-brown bed bug in side view on pale skin with fine hairs; not visibly feeding (don't say it is biting). No date or photographer on PHIL. Donated by the WHO but marked public domain by PHIL: credit 'CDC / World Health Organization' as the ledger does. The lead option for what-do-bed-bug-bites-look-like (it shows the biter on skin, with no doubt about the identification). Two PHIL photos of bed bugs feeding on an arm were refused (see gaps).
candidates.note: Credit: CDC/ Donated by the World Health Organization, Geneva, Switzerland. (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov). Licence: public-domain. Size: 1200x790.

candidates.confidence: medium-high: a photo credited to a physician and labeled bed bug bites; how the cause was established is not stated
candidates.sourceDescription: Wikimedia Commons 'Bedbugb2.JPG', own work by James Heilman, MD (User:Jmh649), 2013-05-08 11:05:18, CC BY-SA 3.0; description 'Bedbug bites'. Taken 23 seconds after 'Bedbugb1.JPG' (same camera), which has been on file since batch 2 as bed-bug-bites-forearm: the same set.
candidates.caveats: Red, raised welts scattered over a person's upper back and shoulders, some in small groups. The description is two words: say 'bed bug bites (photo: James Heilman, MD)' and don't add a diagnosis story. Same set as bed-bug-bites-forearm: don't present them as two people. CC BY-SA 3.0: credit, and share-alike applies to the image file.
candidates.note: Credit: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0. Size: 1200x1248.

candidates.confidence: medium: the photographer attributes his own bites to bed bugs; no clinical confirmation
candidates.sourceDescription: Wikimedia Commons 'Bed bug bites around left wrist.jpg', own work by Oliver Arend (User:Raketenolli), 2013-07-29, CC BY-SA 3.0. Description: 'Approx. four day old bed bug bites on the outside of the left arm, around the wrist', followed by general text with errors and a link to a commercial bed bug site; German: 'Ca. vier Tage alte Bettwanzen-Bisse auf der Außenseite des linken Arms'.
candidates.caveats: A line of small red bumps along the outside of the forearm toward the wrist: the 'row of bites' pattern people search for. Write 'bites the photographer attributes to bed bugs'. The rest of the Commons description is wrong in places ('Bed Bugs can sting') and promotional: never quote it (photos.json keeps its first 300 characters as the source's text). CC BY-SA 3.0: credit Oliver Arend.
candidates.note: Credit: Oliver Arend, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0. Size: 1200x2051.

candidates.confidence: clinical record: CDC attributes the papules to imported fire ants (species unknown)
candidates.sourceDescription: CDC PHIL 16368, content provider CDC/John Ridley, Department of Agriculture, Capitol Square, Atlanta, Georgia; public domain per PHIL. Description: 'erythematous papules, which were the result of this individual having been bitten by imported fire ants ... In this particular instance, it is not known, which species was responsible.'
candidates.caveats: A close-up of five or six raised, shiny, pale pustule-like bumps on reddened skin, the skin's fine grid visible; no body part or date. PHIL says 'bitten'; fire ants grip with their jaws and sting (cite a source): on the page call them stings. Say 'imported fire ants' unless naming both species with a source. Public domain: the lead option for fire-ant-stings.
candidates.note: Credit: CDC/ John Ridley, Department of Agriculture, Capitol Square, Atlanta, Georgia (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov). Licence: public-domain. Size: 1200x790.

candidates.sourceDescription: CDC PHIL 25047, content provider CDC/Harold George Scott, PhD; public domain per PHIL. Description: 'both lower legs of a male patient demonstrating multiple maculopapular and pustular lesions consistent with fire ant stings caused by Solenopsis saevissima ... Note the erythematous halo surrounding each pustular center.' PHIL 25044 to 25046 are more views of the same patient.
candidates.caveats: Both lower legs against a dark blue backdrop with scattered red spots, a few with pale centers: shows how the stings scatter over the legs. PHIL's 'Solenopsis saevissima' is the older name it uses for the imported fire ants (cite a source before giving the current names). No date given. Use one of the three PHIL fire ant photos per page section.
candidates.note: Credit: CDC/ Harold George Scott, PhD (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov). Licence: public-domain. Size: 1200x1097.

candidates.sourceDescription: CDC PHIL 15978, content provider CDC/Harold George Scott, PhD; public domain per PHIL. Description: 'The arm of this patient displayed a number of erythematous pustular lesions that had been caused by the bites of fire ants, Solenopsis saevissima ... Note the erythematous ring, which surrounded the pustular, papular center.'
candidates.caveats: A hairy arm on a black backdrop with several small pustules ringed in red. The single pustule is clearer in fire-ant-sting-pustule (PHIL 6347, on file since batch 3) and fire-ant-stings-pustules-closeup. Same wording point as above ('stings').
candidates.note: Credit: CDC/ Harold George Scott, PhD (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov). Licence: public-domain. Size: 1200x1400.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 238169041, Blount County, Alabama, 2024-08-26, by Kristi Zoebelein (kzoebel; about 49,000 observations). Observer's note: 'I watched it walk on my hand and then it just bit me randomly.' Identified as Camponotus pennsylvanicus by the observer and mettcollsuss (Emmett Collins-Sussman, about 527,000 identifications). Photo 1 of 2; CC0.
candidates.caveats: A large black carpenter ant walking across the fingers of a hand: the ant against fingers gives the scale. The bite is the observer's report; no bite mark shows: 'a carpenter ant that bit the observer moments later'. CC0 and confidently identified: the lead option for do-carpenter-ants-bite.

candidates.sourceDescription: iNaturalist research-grade observation 227695136, Saratoga, California, 2024-07-01, by bungelina. Observer's note: 'In the last two photos you can see the larvae and some of the unhatched eggs in the cells. The homeowners plan to leave the nest alone. The wasps have been building for decades under the overhang of the house, and they never seem to get very large or be a problem.' Identified as Polistes dominula by the observer and Ruan Veldtman (ruanveldt, about 23,000 identifications). Photo 1 of 4.
candidates.caveats: An open, umbrella-shaped paper comb with five or six European paper wasps on it, in the angle where a white wall meets the underside of the roof overhang; some white-capped cells. 'Never a problem' is these homeowners' experience, not advice: don't use it to say nests are harmless. CC BY: credit bungelina.
candidates.note: Credit: (c) bungelina, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist. Licence: CC-BY-4.0. Size: 1200x800.

Observer's note: 'On the back interior wall and ceiling of garage'. Identified as Sceliphron caementarium by the observer and philipwoodscc (Philip Woods, about 324,000 identifications). Photo 2 of 8.
candidates.caveats: A black-and-yellow mud dauber (yellow legs, thread waist) on a rounded mud cell with an open hole at one end, on white painted wood inside a garage. Sex not recorded (only females build: cite a source before saying 'female'). CC BY: credit Randy A Nonenmacher.

Observer's note: 'We have been getting one nest per year on our house for the last few years, but this really seems to be the most successful one yet- the others only seemed to be a couple chambers, but this seems to have several.' Identified as Sceliphron caementarium by the observer and jfmantis (Julian Fuchs, about 368,000 identifications). Field 'Urban / Built Environment': yes. Photo 5 of 7.
candidates.caveats: A mud dauber on top of a lumpy mud nest of several cells, one sealed cell end showing as a dark round cap, on a white ledge under a light fixture (a white dome behind). The wasp is slightly soft; the nest on the house is the subject. CC BY: credit Heather Dawnstar Sabin.
